blocks.html: How do we know what happened at Jamestown in 1607 or in Philadelphia in 1776? Nobody alive today was there. Historians work like careful detectives: they gather evidence left behind by the past and reason from it. The first question to ask about any piece of evidence is simple: who made it, and when?

A primary source was made at the time, by someone who saw or took part in the events: a letter, a diary, a law, a map, a speech, a photograph, a tool dug from the ground. A secondary source was made later by someone studying the events from other sources: a textbook, a history book, a documentary.

The line between the two is about distance from the event, not age. A primary source lets you hear a voice from the time, with its details, its feelings and its blind spots. A secondary source steps back: its author has read many primary sources, compared them and offers an explanation. Historians need both. Primary sources are the raw evidence; secondary sources are arguments built from that evidence, and they can be checked against it.

steps: Ask when it was made: 1910.
Ask when the events happened: Jamestown was founded in 1607, about 300 years earlier.
Ask who made it: an author who studied records, not someone who was there.
blocks.a: A secondary source. It is old, but it was made long after the events by someone studying them.

blocks.title: Primary or secondary?
blocks.q: The Mayflower Compact, the agreement the Pilgrim men signed on board their ship in November 1620.
steps: When was it made? In 1620, at the very moment it describes.
Who made it? The people who were forming the government.
blocks.a: A primary source: it was made by participants, at the time.

blocks.html: Two mix-ups are common. First, calling anything old a primary source: a 1910 history of the Revolution is old, but secondary. Second, treating a primary source as true because it was there. When Christopher Columbus wrote in 1493 that the island people he met had "no kind of government," he could not speak their language and had stayed only a short time. His letter is excellent evidence of what Columbus believed and wanted his readers to think; it is weak evidence about Taíno government. Check every source, primary or secondary, against others.

Some sources can be both, depending on your question. Mercy Otis Warren lived through the Revolution and published a history of it in 1805. For the events of the war, her book is a secondary history; for how a Patriot writer of the time saw the war, it is a primary source.

blocks.html: In Primary and Secondary Sources you learned to ask who made a source and when. Now go one step further. Every source was made by a person, at a moment, for someone, for a reason. Historians call this sourcing. The AP U.S. History exam asks about four parts of it, which many teachers remember as HIPP.

blocks.html: HIPP asks why a source says what it says. The situation, the audience, the purpose and the author's point of view shape what a source includes, what it stresses and what it leaves out.

A source is not a window onto the past; it is a message from one person to others. A general writes one way to his commander and another way to his family. Knowing the message's setting lets you use it fairly: you can trust it most on what the author was in a position to know and had little reason to bend, and read it more carefully where the author had a reason to persuade.

blocks.q: In October 1765 the Stamp Act Congress declared that colonists owed "the same allegiance to the crown" as people in Britain, and also that no taxes should be laid on them "but with their own consent." Why both?

P: To win repeal of the tax without being treated as rebels.
blocks.a: Loyal words to a powerful audience made the protest harder to dismiss. The loyalty was also real: most colonists in 1765 wanted their rights inside the empire, not independence.

blocks.html: The most common slip is to summarize a source and stop. "Columbus says he found many islands" is a summary. Sourcing asks why he wrote it that way and for whom. The opposite slip is to throw out a source because it has a point of view. Every source has one; a biased source is still evidence, at least of what its author believed or wanted others to believe.

blocks.html: History runs on dates, and dates are easy to slip on. All the dates in this course are AD, counted forward from the traditional year of Jesus's birth; years BC count backward before it. A decade is ten years ("the 1760s" means 1760 to 1769), and a century is one hundred years.
The 18th century is the 1700s. To name a century from a year, take the hundreds part and add one: 1776 → 17 + 1 → the 18th century. In strict counting, the 18th century runs from 1701 to 1800.

There was no year zero. The first century AD was the years 1 through 100, so the second century began in 101, and so on. By the time the calendar reached the 1700s, people were already in the 18th hundred years. That is why the number of the century is always one ahead of the hundreds digits. Everyday speech uses "the 1700s" for 1700 to 1799, which matches the strict 18th century for every year except the round ones like 1700 and 1800.

blocks.html: Historians also group years into periods that begin and end at turning points. The AP U.S. History course uses nine. This course covers the first three in this half: Period 1 (1491 to 1607), Period 2 (1607 to 1754) and Period 3 (1754 to 1800). Each start date marks a change: contact between hemispheres, the first lasting English colony, and the war that set Britain and its colonies on the road to revolution.

blocks.html: Once events are in order (Dates, Centuries and Periods), historians ask the big questions: why did this happen, what did it lead to, and what changed or stayed the same? These are the reasoning skills behind nearly every essay question in U.S. history.

Big events usually have several causes: long-term causes (conditions that built up over years) and short-term causes or triggers (the sparks just before). They also have several effects, some intended and some not.

A spark only starts a fire where there is fuel. The shots at Lexington in April 1775 did not cause the Revolution by themselves; a hundred and fifty years of colonial self-government, new British taxes after 1763 and ten years of protest had built up the fuel. Separating long-term conditions from short-term triggers explains both why something happened and why then.

blocks.title: Long-term or short-term?
blocks.q: Is "Britain's war debt after 1763" a long-term or short-term cause of the Revolution?
steps: Ask how far before 1775 it began: about twelve years.
Ask what it set in motion: new taxes (1764 to 1767) and protests.
It is not the spark itself, but it is much closer than the century of self-government.
blocks.a: A medium-to-short-term cause: it led directly to the taxes that started the quarrel. Historians may label it either way; what matters is explaining how it led to the war.

blocks.title: Did it cause it?
blocks.q: The Great Awakening (1730s and 1740s) came before the Revolution (1775). Did it cause the Revolution?
steps: Coming before is not enough: many things came before 1775.
Look for a link: the Awakening taught many colonists to question established church leaders and to choose for themselves.
Then weigh it: historians debate how much that habit carried over into politics.
blocks.a: It may be one long-term influence among several, but "it came first" alone proves nothing.

blocks.html: Historians also study continuity and change over time. After the Revolution, the new states wrote constitutions and some Northern states began to end slavery (change); most states still let only men who owned property vote (continuity). Asking both questions keeps the picture honest.

The two classic errors: naming one cause for a big event, and assuming that whatever came just before an event caused it (logicians call this "after this, therefore because of this"). Check for a link you can explain: how, step by step, did the cause lead to the effect?

blocks.html: The story of America does not begin in 1492 or 1607. People had lived in the Americas for thousands of years before any European arrived. How do we know, when those first peoples left no writing? This is a good test of the skills from the last unit: historians and archaeologists reason from evidence such as stone tools, hearths, bones, footprints and DNA.

People reached the Americas from northeast Asia during the last Ice Age, at least 15,000 years ago. They came by land across Beringia, along the Pacific coast, or both. Exactly when, and by which route, is still studied and debated.

During the Ice Age, so much water was locked in glaciers that the sea was far lower than today. A wide land, Beringia, joined Siberia and Alaska where the Bering Strait is now. People and animals could live there and move east. As the ice melted, the sea rose and covered the land bridge, between about 13,000 and 11,500 years ago. Two routes south are proposed: an inland corridor that opened between melting ice sheets, and a coastal route by boat or on foot along the Pacific shore, with fish and shellfish for food.

blocks.title: Using a dated site
blocks.q: Monte Verde, in southern Chile, has tools and hearths dated to at least 14,500 years ago. What does that tell us about when people first entered the Americas?
steps: Chile is at the far southern end of South America, thousands of miles from Beringia.
People had to travel all that way before they could camp at Monte Verde.
So people must have entered the Americas some time before 14,500 years ago.
blocks.a: People entered the Americas earlier than 14,500 years ago; a far-south site pushes the date of first arrival back.

blocks.title: Why a route matters
blocks.q: Many coastal sites from the Ice Age would be under water today. How does that affect the debate over the coastal route?
steps: The sea rose as the ice melted, so the old shoreline is now offshore.
Evidence of a coastal route would mostly be drowned.
So a lack of coastal sites does not prove no one used the coast.
blocks.a: Missing evidence is weak evidence: the coastal route is hard to test, which is one reason it is still debated.

blocks.html: For many years, the Clovis culture (named for stone spear points found near Clovis, New Mexico, about 13,000 years old) was thought to be the first. Older sites such as Monte Verde changed that view. Many Native nations also hold their own origin accounts, passed down for generations, which carry deep meaning for those nations; this course describes the archaeological evidence.

Students often learn one date and one route as if they were settled. Archaeologists agree that people came from northeast Asia over thousands of years; they debate the earliest date and the routes, and each newly dated site can shift the picture. When you write about it, say "at least 15,000 years ago" and name the debate.

blocks.html: By 1491, millions of people lived in North America, speaking hundreds of languages in many separate nations. Their ancestors had arrived thousands of years earlier (The First Peoples of the Americas) and spread across a continent with deserts, prairies, rain forests and woodlands. Each people built a way of life that fit its land.

Native societies adapted to their environments: farming and irrigation in the Southwest, bison hunting and river farming on the Plains, fishing (especially salmon) on the Pacific Northwest coast, and mixed farming, hunting and villages in the Eastern Woodlands.

Before trade with Europe, a people lived mostly from what its own region could provide. Rain, soil, growing season and the plants and animals nearby set what was possible. Where rivers could water fields, people farmed; where salmon ran every year, people fished and stored food; where great bison herds grazed, people hunted them. The same need, food and shelter, led to different answers in different places.

blocks.html: A familiar picture of Plains peoples on horseback chasing bison is from after contact. There were no horses in the Americas in 1491; the Spanish brought them. Horses spread north after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, and the great horse cultures of the Plains grew in the 1700s. In 1491, Plains peoples hunted on foot.

blocks.html: Some Native peoples built towns, monuments and alliances on a large scale, long before Europeans arrived. Three examples, building on Native Cultures Across North America, show how much they achieved.

Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was the largest city of the Mississippian culture (about 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1100). The Ancestral Puebloans of the Four Corners built great houses at Chaco Canyon and cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde. The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy joined five nations under a shared council and the Great Law of Peace.

Farming made these societies possible. Maize, beans and squash grown in surplus fed people who could then build mounds, trade over long distances and govern large populations. Large towns and alliances needed leaders, rules and ways to settle disputes, so these peoples built political systems as well as buildings.

blocks.cap: Cahokia lies across the Mississippi from St. Louis; Mesa Verde is in southwestern Colorado, in the Four Corners region.

items: Cahokia (about 900 to 1400, at its height about 1050 to 1350): more than 100 earthen mounds. Monks Mound, about 100 feet tall, is the largest earthen mound built in North America before Columbus. Trade brought copper and shells from far away. The city declined after about 1350, for reasons still studied, such as floods and strain on resources.

Ancestral Puebloans: at Chaco Canyon (about 850 to 1150) they built multistory great houses joined by long roads. At Mesa Verde they built about 600 cliff dwellings, mostly between about 1190 and 1280; Cliff Palace has about 150 rooms. Drought and other pressures led people to move south by about 1300. Today's Pueblo peoples are their descendants.

Haudenosaunee, "People of the Longhouse": the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, joined by the Tuscarora about 1722 (the Six Nations). The Great Law of Peace, kept in memory and recorded with wampum belts, set up a Grand Council of chiefs from the nations.

blocks.html: A common assumption is that large towns and organized governments came to America only from Europe. Cahokia may have been as large as many European towns of its day, and the Haudenosaunee had a working confederacy with a council and rules for peace. Historians do debate one related claim: how much the Haudenosaunee influenced the U.S. Constitution. Congress praised that influence in a 1988 resolution; some historians argue it was large, others that the framers drew mostly on English and colonial models.

blocks.html: In the 1400s, the peoples of the Americas and of Europe, Africa and Asia had no contact with each other (apart from brief Norse visits to Newfoundland about AD 1000). Then, within a few decades, sailors from Portugal and Spain crossed the oceans. Why then, and why them? Use the long-term and short-term causes from Causes, Effects and Change Over Time.

Portugal and Spain explored to reach Asian trade by sea, win wealth, spread Christianity and gain glory for their rulers. Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean on October 12, 1492. The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) split the lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal.

Spices, silk and other goods from Asia were worth a fortune in Europe, but they came overland and through many middlemen, so prices were high. A sea route straight to Asia would cut out the middlemen. New ships (the small, nimble caravel), the compass and the astrolabe made long voyages possible. Kings and queens competed for the profits and the prestige, and many sailors and priests saw spreading their faith as a duty.

blocks.title: Two routes to Asia
blocks.q: Portugal sailed south and east around Africa. Why did Spain back Columbus's plan to sail west?
steps: Portugal already led the route around Africa (Dias, 1488).
Columbus believed Asia lay a short way west across the Atlantic; he underestimated the size of the Earth.
Spain's rulers, Ferdinand and Isabella, wanted their own route and profits.
blocks.a: Spain needed a route of its own, and Columbus promised a shorter one.

blocks.title: Reading Tordesillas
blocks.q: The Treaty of Tordesillas (June 7, 1494) drew a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. Lands to the west went to Spain, lands to the east to Portugal. Which part of South America fell to Portugal?
steps: The line ran north and south through the Atlantic.
The eastern bulge of South America lay east of the line.
Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed it for Portugal in 1500.
blocks.a: Brazil. That is why Brazilians speak Portuguese while most of Latin America speaks Spanish.

blocks.html: Columbus made four voyages between 1492 and 1504. When he landed in the Bahamas, he met the Taíno people. He called them "Indians" because he believed he was in the Indies, near Asia. He died in 1506 still believing he had reached Asia. His voyages began lasting contact between the hemispheres, with huge effects, good and terrible, that the next topics trace.

Europeans did not set out to find two unknown continents. Columbus was trying to reach Asia by sailing west. The name "America" came later, from the mapmakers who used the name of Amerigo Vespucci, who argued the lands were a new world. Also, Columbus did not "discover" a land no one knew: millions of people already lived there.

blocks.html: Columbus's voyages (Why Europeans Explored) did more than open a sea route. For millions of years the two hemispheres had developed separate plants, animals and germs. After 1492, ships carried them across the ocean in both directions. The historian Alfred Crosby named this the Columbian Exchange in 1972.

After 1492, plants, animals, people and diseases crossed the Atlantic both ways. Horses, cattle, pigs, wheat and sugarcane came to the Americas; maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao and tobacco went to Europe, Africa and Asia. Diseases such as smallpox killed a very large share of Native peoples.

Native peoples had never been exposed to smallpox, measles or influenza, so their bodies had no defenses against them. Epidemics swept through towns, often ahead of the Europeans themselves. The crops moved the other way and changed diets around the world: the potato fed northern Europe, maize spread through Africa and China, and the tomato became central to Italian cooking.

blocks.title: Why did the population fall so far?
blocks.q: Estimates of how many Native people died in the first century after contact range from about half to about 90 percent. What was the main cause?
steps: War and forced labor killed many, but they cannot explain deaths in places Europeans had not yet reached.
Diseases new to the Americas spread from person to person and town to town.
People had no immunity, so death rates were very high.
blocks.a: Epidemic disease was the main cause, made worse by war, forced labor and hunger.

blocks.title: An effect far away
blocks.q: How did the Columbian Exchange help cause the Atlantic slave trade to grow?
steps: Sugarcane, brought to the Caribbean and Brazil, grew well there.
Sugar plantations needed huge amounts of hard labor.
With Native populations collapsing, planters bought enslaved Africans by the millions.
blocks.a: Sugar and the loss of Native workers drove demand for enslaved labor from Africa.

blocks.html: People crossed too. Europeans came as settlers and soldiers, and millions of Africans were carried across the Atlantic in chains. Scholars debate some details, such as whether syphilis traveled from the Americas to Europe (recent studies of ancient DNA support that view) and how large the 1491 population was. The broad pattern is not in doubt.

Two errors are common. One: thinking the exchange went only one way, from Europe to America. Crops from the Americas changed the whole world's food. Two: thinking Native peoples died mostly in battle. War mattered, but disease caused most of the deaths.

blocks.html: Spain moved fast after the first contacts. Within fifty years of 1492, small Spanish forces had toppled the two largest empires in the Americas and built an empire that would last three centuries.

Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec (Mexica) capital, Tenochtitlan, in 1521; Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532. Spain ruled through the encomienda system and Catholic missions, founded St. Augustine, Florida, in 1565, and argued over how Native peoples should be treated.

How could a few hundred Spaniards defeat empires of millions? Steel, horses and guns gave them an edge in battle, but three other things were decisive. Native allies: peoples conquered by the Aztecs, above all the Tlaxcalans, joined Cortés by the tens of thousands. Disease: smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520 and killed the Aztec ruler Cuitláhuac. Division: the Inca Empire had just fought a civil war between the brothers Atahualpa and Huáscar.

blocks.title: Explain the conquest
blocks.q: Name three reasons the siege of Tenochtitlan ended in Spanish victory in August 1521.
steps: Allies: Tlaxcalans and other Native peoples who resented Aztec rule fought alongside the Spanish.
Disease: the smallpox epidemic of 1520 had killed many people, including the ruler.
Siege: boats with cannons controlled the lake, and the city was cut off from food.
blocks.a: Native allies, disease and a siege that starved the city, along with Spanish weapons.

blocks.title: The encomienda
blocks.q: Under the encomienda, the Spanish crown "entrusted" groups of Native people to a colonist. What did that mean in practice?
steps: The colonist was to protect them and teach them Christianity.
In return he could demand their labor and tribute.
In practice it often meant forced, deadly work in mines and fields.
blocks.a: A grant of Native labor and tribute that led to widespread abuse.

blocks.html: Some Spaniards protested. The priest Bartolomé de las Casas, once an encomienda holder himself, spent decades denouncing the abuses. The crown's New Laws of 1542 banned new encomiendas and the enslavement of Native people, though colonists resisted and abuses went on. In the Valladolid debate (1550 to 1551), Las Casas argued against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda that Native peoples were fully rational people with rights. Las Casas had at first suggested using enslaved Africans instead, a view he later rejected as equally unjust.

In what is now the United States, Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest continuously occupied European-founded city in the country, and New Mexico (Juan de Oñate's expedition of 1598; Santa Fe in 1610), with missions to convert the Pueblo peoples.

The legend says a handful of brave soldiers conquered empires by themselves. Native allies, epidemics and divisions within the Aztec and Inca states were decisive. A second mistake is to treat "the Spanish" as all of one mind: the empire's own priests and lawyers argued fiercely about its treatment of Native peoples.

blocks.html: Spain had built an empire in the Americas (The Spanish Empire in the Americas). England came later. Its first lasting colony was Jamestown, founded in May 1607 on the James River in Virginia by the Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock company whose investors hoped for gold and quick profits.

Jamestown nearly failed, then grew rich on tobacco. In 1619 Virginia held the first meeting of the House of Burgesses, the first elected assembly in English America, and the first recorded Africans arrived in the colony.

The settlers chose a swampy site that was easy to defend but had bad water and disease. Many were gentlemen unused to farming, and they depended on corn traded from the Powhatan Confederacy, whose lands they had entered. Hunger, disease and conflict killed most early colonists. In the "starving time" (winter 1609 to 1610), only about 60 of some 500 people survived. Two changes saved the colony. John Rolfe began growing a sweet tobacco about 1612 that sold well in England. And under the headright system (from 1618), anyone who paid for a person's passage got 50 acres, which drew thousands of indentured servants to work the tobacco fields.

blocks.title: Why tobacco mattered
blocks.q: How did tobacco change who came to Virginia?
steps: Tobacco sold for good prices in England, so planters wanted more land and more workers.
The headright system gave 50 acres for each person whose passage a planter paid.
Planters paid the passage of poor English men and women, who worked as indentured servants for several years.
blocks.a: Tobacco and headrights drew thousands of young indentured servants and made land the road to wealth.

blocks.title: Read the year 1619
blocks.q: Two events of 1619 point toward later American history. What are they?
steps: July 30, 1619: the House of Burgesses meets, with burgesses chosen by the colonists.
August 1619: "20 and odd" Africans, captured in Angola, are brought to Point Comfort and sold.
blocks.a: Self-government and African bondage began in English America in the same year.

blocks.html: Conflict with the Powhatan peoples grew as tobacco farms spread over their lands. In 1622, under Opechancanough, they attacked the English settlements and killed 347 colonists, between a quarter and a third of them; the English answered with years of war. In 1624 the king took over the struggling company, and Virginia became a royal colony.

Jamestown did not thrive from the start. Most early settlers died, and the colony was nearly abandoned in 1610. It lasted because of tobacco, headrights and new supplies of people. A second error: the Africans of 1619 are sometimes described as free servants and sometimes as enslaved. They had been captured and sold; their exact legal status in Virginia's early years is debated, and laws making slavery lifelong and inherited came later, in the 1660s.

blocks.html: Thirteen years after Jamestown, a very different group sailed for America. They came not for gold but for their faith. Young learners meet them as the Pilgrims; here is the fuller story.

The Pilgrims, Separatists who had left the Church of England, signed the Mayflower Compact in 1620 and founded Plymouth. The Puritans, who hoped to purify the church from within, founded Massachusetts Bay in 1630. Dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson were banished, and Williams founded Rhode Island in 1636.

The Mayflower landed at Cape Cod, outside the area its charter covered, so the passengers had no legal government. Before going ashore, 41 men signed a compact to form a "civil Body Politick" and obey its laws. It was a small step, but it showed a habit that would matter: people agreeing to govern themselves. About half the Pilgrims died that first winter. The Wampanoag leader Massasoit (Ousamequin) made an alliance with them in 1621, and Tisquantum (Squanto), who spoke English, taught them to plant corn.

blocks.html: The Puritans of Massachusetts Bay came in much larger numbers: about 20,000 in the "Great Migration" of the 1630s, mostly in families. Their governor, John Winthrop, told them they would be watched by the world:

blocks.title: Why were dissenters banished?
blocks.q: Roger Williams taught that the government should not punish people for their religious beliefs and that the colonists should buy land from the Native peoples. Why did Massachusetts banish him in 1635?
steps: The Puritans had come to build a community that followed their faith.
They believed the government should uphold true religion and that dissent threatened the whole community.
Williams challenged both the colony's church rules and its land claims.
blocks.a: He threatened the order they had crossed an ocean to build. He went south and founded Providence (1636), where no one was punished for religion.

blocks.title: Another dissenter
blocks.q: Anne Hutchinson held meetings in her home where she questioned ministers' teaching. What happened?
steps: She was tried in 1637 and banished in 1638.
She moved to Rhode Island, which had become a home for dissenters.
blocks.a: Banished; she settled in Rhode Island.

blocks.html: New England grew as a land of towns, churches, small farms, fishing and trade. Town meetings ran local affairs. A Massachusetts law of 1647 required towns to keep schools, so that children could read the Bible. Connecticut's settlers wrote the Fundamental Orders (1639), a written plan of government.

A popular idea is that the Puritans came to found a land of religious freedom for everyone. They sought freedom to practice their own faith, and they expected others in their colony to conform. Religious toleration came from dissenters like Williams, not from the Puritan leaders.

blocks.html: Between New England and the Chesapeake lay the Middle colonies: New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware. Not all of them began as English colonies, and none was settled by a single church.

The Middle colonies were the most diverse. New York began as Dutch New Netherland and became English in 1664. William Penn, a Quaker, founded Pennsylvania in 1681 with wide religious freedom. Rich soil made the region the colonies' "breadbasket," growing wheat for export through ports such as New York and Philadelphia.

The Dutch West India Company cared most about the fur trade and welcomed settlers of many backgrounds to make the colony pay. After England took it, the mix remained. Penn, for his part, wanted a "holy experiment": Quakers had been jailed in England for their beliefs, so he promised freedom of worship to all who believed in God. That promise drew English and Welsh Quakers, Germans of many churches, Scots-Irish Presbyterians and others. Diversity came both from trade and from principle.

blocks.title: New Netherland becomes New York
blocks.q: How did New Netherland become New York?
steps: The Dutch had built New Amsterdam on Manhattan, which Peter Minuit bought from Lenape people in 1626 for trade goods.
In 1664, during a war between England and the Netherlands, English warships arrived.
Governor Peter Stuyvesant surrendered without a battle, and the colony was renamed for the Duke of York.
blocks.a: England took it in 1664 without a fight, and the Dutch settlers stayed.

blocks.title: Why Pennsylvania?
blocks.q: King Charles II gave William Penn a huge grant of land in 1681. Why?
steps: The crown owed a large debt to Penn's late father, an admiral.
The land grant paid it off, and it also gave England a place to send Quakers.
blocks.a: To repay a royal debt; Penn turned it into a refuge for Quakers and others.

blocks.html: Penn planned Philadelphia, the "City of Brotherly Love," and made treaties with the Lenape to buy land; later deals, such as the Walking Purchase of 1737, cheated the Lenape and broke that early peace. Delaware, first settled as New Sweden (1638), was governed with Pennsylvania until it got its own assembly in the early 1700s. New Jersey was split off from New York in 1664.

blocks.html: Students often assume every colony was English from the start and that all colonies were alike. New York began as Dutch, Delaware as Swedish, and the Middle colonies mixed Dutch, English, German, Scots-Irish and other settlers, with Quakers, Lutherans, Presbyterians, Catholics, Jews and others living side by side.

blocks.html: South of Pennsylvania, the long growing season and rich coastal soil shaped colonies built on cash crops. Virginia (Jamestown and the Chesapeake) was the first; four more followed.

Maryland (1634) was founded by the Calverts as a refuge for English Catholics. The Carolinas (charter 1663) grew rice and indigo on plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Georgia (charter 1732) was the last of the thirteen colonies.

Each Southern colony was a proprietary grant: the king gave land and power to an owner or group of owners, who hoped to profit from rents and trade. Their plans shaped the colonies at first, but the land shaped them more. Crops that sold well in Europe, such as tobacco, rice and indigo, needed many workers, and planters turned more and more to enslaved Africans.

items: Maryland: granted in 1632 to the Calvert family (Lords Baltimore), settled in 1634. Protestants soon outnumbered Catholics, so in 1649 the assembly passed the Toleration Act, protecting Christians who believed in the Trinity. Like Virginia, it grew tobacco.

The Carolinas: granted in 1663 to eight Lords Proprietors. Many early settlers of Charles Town (Charleston), founded in 1670, came from Barbados, an English sugar island built on slavery, and brought its slave laws. Rice became South Carolina's great crop, and indigo (for blue dye) another. Carolina traders also captured and sold Native people as slaves. North and South Carolina became separate colonies in the early 1700s.

Georgia: chartered in 1732 for trustees led by James Oglethorpe; Savannah was founded the next year. Georgia was to be a buffer against Spanish Florida and a fresh start for poor English families. The trustees at first banned slavery; under pressure from settlers, the ban ended in 1751, and rice plantations spread.

blocks.title: Why Georgia?
blocks.q: Name two reasons Britain founded Georgia in the 1730s.
steps: Look at the map: Georgia lies between South Carolina and Spanish Florida.
Read the founders' aims: Oglethorpe wanted a fresh start for poor English families.
blocks.a: To guard South Carolina against Spanish Florida, and to give poor settlers a new start.

blocks.title: Who lived in the South?
blocks.q: In the 1700s, did most white Southerners own large plantations?
steps: Large plantations needed money for land and enslaved workers.
Most white families farmed small plots, often without enslaved workers.
A small group of wealthy planters owned most of the enslaved people and much of the best land.
blocks.a: No. Most were small farmers; the planter elite was small but powerful.

blocks.html: A common picture has every Southern colonist living on a plantation. Most white Southerners were small farmers, and the large plantations, which held most of the enslaved people, belonged to a wealthy few. Another slip: Maryland was founded as a Catholic refuge, but Protestants were a majority there from early on.

blocks.html: You have met all three regions: New England, the Middle colonies and the South. AP questions often ask you to compare them and, above all, to explain why they differed.

New England: towns, churches, small farms, fishing, shipbuilding and trade. Middle colonies: wheat farms, busy ports and the most diverse people and faiths. Southern colonies: cash crops (tobacco, rice, indigo), plantations and slavery. Geography and the settlers' goals explain the differences.

Start with the land. New England has rocky soil, hills and short summers, but good harbors, forests and rich fishing grounds, so people farmed small plots and turned to the sea. The Middle colonies have fertile valleys and a mild climate that grow wheat well, and wide rivers that carried it to port. The South has a long growing season and flat, wet coastal land, ideal for tobacco and rice, crops that paid best when grown on large plantations with many workers. Then add the settlers: Puritan families in New England built close-knit towns around churches; Penn's promise of religious freedom drew a mix of peoples to the Middle colonies; Southern planters sought profit and bought enslaved labor.

blocks.title: Explain a difference
blocks.q: Why did slavery grow much larger in South Carolina than in Massachusetts, though it was legal in both?
steps: Rice in South Carolina needed many workers in hot, wet fields all year.
Massachusetts farms were small, and its trades needed fewer field workers.
So planters in the South bought enslaved Africans in large numbers; in Massachusetts, enslaved people were fewer and worked mostly in homes, shops and ports.
blocks.a: The crop and the land made the demand for labor very different.

blocks.html: Students often sort colonies by one memorized fact ("Pennsylvania = Quakers"). That works until a question asks why. Tie each region's economy to its land and climate, then to its settlers. Remember too that regions overlapped: there were merchants in Charleston and enslaved people in New York.

blocks.html: Slavery shaped every English colony. This topic tells its colonial history plainly. Building on The Southern Colonies, it explains how slavery grew, how it was written into law, and how enslaved people resisted.

About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships in the Atlantic slave trade, and about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage; under 5 percent of them came to the mainland colonies. Colonial slave codes made slavery lifelong and inherited through the mother. Enslaved people resisted in many ways, including the Stono Rebellion of 1739.

At first, Chesapeake planters relied mostly on English indentured servants, who worked for some years and then went free. Late in the 1600s that supply fell, and freed servants wanted land of their own. Planters turned to enslaved Africans, who could be held for life. Laws followed the economy: in 1662, Virginia declared that a child would be "bond or free only according to the condition of the mother," so the children of enslaved women were enslaved from birth. By 1705, Virginia's slave code treated enslaved people as property. By 1775, about 500,000 people, about one in five people in the colonies, were enslaved.

blocks.html: The Middle Passage was the voyage from West and Central Africa to the Americas. Captives were chained below deck in crowded, airless holds for weeks; between one and two in every ten died on the way. Most were carried to Brazil and the Caribbean.

blocks.title: Resistance
blocks.q: How did enslaved people resist slavery?
steps: Every day: working slowly, breaking tools, keeping their own music, faith and family ties.
Escape: some fled, for example to Spanish Florida, where Spain offered freedom to those who accepted Catholicism.
Revolt: in 1739, about twenty enslaved men near the Stono River in South Carolina seized guns and marched south toward Florida, gathering others, before the militia defeated them.
blocks.a: In daily life, by escape and by armed revolt.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.q: What did South Carolina do after the Stono Rebellion?
steps: Planters feared more revolts in a colony where enslaved people were the majority.
The Negro Act of 1740 barred enslaved people from learning to read, gathering in groups or moving about freely.
blocks.a: It passed a harsher slave code, the Negro Act of 1740.

blocks.html: Two mistakes are common. First, slavery was not only Southern: it was legal in all thirteen colonies, and enslaved people worked in Boston, Newport and New York City. Second, slavery was not fixed in law from 1619. The laws that made it lifelong and inherited came step by step, beginning in the 1660s.

blocks.html: As the colonies of all three regions grew, they pressed onto Native lands. Native nations traded, allied, negotiated and, when those failed, fought. Four conflicts of the 1600s show the pattern and its variety.

The Pequot War (1636 to 1638) and King Philip's (Metacom's) War (1675 to 1676) in New England; Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia (1676), an uprising of colonists against their governor; and the Pueblo Revolt (1680), which drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years.

The conflicts grew from competition for land, trade and power. English farms and livestock spread over Native fields and hunting grounds; colonial courts favored colonists; disease had already weakened many nations. Native leaders had choices to make: some allied with the English against rivals, some resisted. Colonists were divided too, as Bacon's Rebellion showed.

items: Pequot War: English colonists, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, fought the Pequot. In May 1637 they burned a fortified Pequot village at Mystic, killing some 400 to 700 people, most of them women, children and elders. The Treaty of Hartford (1638) scattered the surviving Pequot.

King Philip's War: Metacom, son of Massasoit and leader of the Wampanoag, led a coalition against the spreading colonies. Dozens of towns were burned and thousands died; measured against population, it was one of the deadliest wars in American history. Metacom was killed in August 1676, and many captives were sold into slavery.

Bacon's Rebellion: Nathaniel Bacon led frontier settlers, including poor freed servants and some enslaved Africans, who were angry that Governor William Berkeley would not wage war on Native peoples to open land. They attacked Native villages, some of them peaceful, and burned Jamestown in September 1676. The revolt collapsed after Bacon died.

Pueblo Revolt: on August 10, 1680, Pueblo peoples led by Popé rose against Spanish forced labor and the suppression of their religion. They drove the Spanish from Santa Fe; Spain did not return until Diego de Vargas's campaign of 1692.

blocks.title: Why does Bacon's Rebellion matter?
blocks.q: Historians often connect Bacon's Rebellion to the growth of slavery in Virginia. What is the link?
steps: Bacon's army joined poor freed servants and some enslaved Africans against the colony's leaders.
Planters grew wary of a large class of poor, armed, landless former servants.
In the following decades they bought more enslaved Africans and fewer indentured servants.
blocks.a: Many historians see it as one reason planters shifted toward slavery; others stress the falling supply of servants. Both factors were at work.

blocks.html: Avoid treating Native nations as only victims or only enemies. Nations chose allies (the Mohegan and Narragansett fought beside the English against the Pequot), traded, negotiated and fought to protect their lands, and the Pueblo Revolt won twelve years of independence. Also, Bacon's Rebellion was a revolt by colonists against their own government, not a war between colonists and one Native nation.

blocks.html: Why did England want colonies at all? The answer is an economic idea that ruled European empires in this era. It links the colonial economies you have studied to the quarrel that would later break the empire apart.

Under mercantilism, colonies existed to make the mother country rich: they supplied raw materials and bought its manufactured goods. The Navigation Acts (from 1651) required colonial trade to go in English ships, and key "enumerated" goods to go only to England or its colonies. For decades Britain enforced these laws loosely, a policy later called salutary neglect.

Mercantilists measured a nation's wealth in gold and silver. A country grew richer when it sold more abroad than it bought, a favorable balance of trade. Colonies helped twice: they produced goods the nation would otherwise buy from rivals (sugar, tobacco, naval stores), and they were a protected market for the nation's cloth and tools. Laws kept that trade, and the shipping profits, inside the empire.

blocks.title: Who gains?
blocks.q: A Virginia planter must ship his tobacco to England, even if Dutch merchants would pay more. Who benefits from the rule?
steps: English merchants and shippers get the trade and can resell tobacco to Europe at a profit.
The English government collects customs duties.
The planter may get a lower price, but his tobacco has a protected market in England.
blocks.a: England gains most; the colonist gains some protection but loses freedom to sell where he likes.

blocks.title: Salutary neglect
blocks.q: Why did Britain enforce the trade laws loosely before 1763?
steps: Prime Minister Robert Walpole (1721 to 1742) thought a growing colonial trade would enrich Britain more than strict enforcement.
Customs officers were few and smuggling was easy along a long coast.
Britain was busy with wars in Europe.
blocks.a: Leniency seemed to pay, and strictness was hard. The phrase "wise and salutary neglect" is Edmund Burke's, from 1775.

blocks.html: Because of this long leniency, colonists grew used to trading, smuggling and governing themselves with little interference. When Britain began enforcing the laws and adding new taxes after 1763, the change felt like an attack on their rights.

Mercantilism is not free trade; it is close to the opposite. Free trade lets merchants buy and sell where they like; mercantilism used laws to steer trade so the mother country came out ahead. Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) was written in large part as a critique of the mercantile system.

blocks.html: In the 1700s two movements swept the colonies and changed how people thought about authority. One was about the heart and faith, the other about reason and science. Both grew from soil prepared by New England's churches and schools.

The First Great Awakening (1730s and 1740s) was a wave of religious revival led by preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield. The Enlightenment stressed reason, science and natural rights, from thinkers such as John Locke, and reached the colonies through books, newspapers, colleges and Benjamin Franklin.

The Awakening taught that each person needed a heartfelt conversion and could judge whether a minister truly preached the gospel. Churches split between "New Lights," who welcomed the revivals, and "Old Lights," who distrusted them. The Enlightenment taught that people could understand the world by reason and that governments exist to protect natural rights. One spoke the language of faith and the other of reason, but both encouraged ordinary colonists to question established authority.

blocks.title: Two movements, one printer
blocks.q: Benjamin Franklin, an Enlightenment man, printed George Whitefield's sermons and became his friend. What does that show?
steps: Franklin admired Whitefield's preaching and his power to draw crowds; he once estimated a crowd in Philadelphia at about 25,000.
Printing the sermons also sold well.
The two movements were different, but people in them mixed, and print spread both.
blocks.a: The movements overlapped in daily life, and newspapers and print carried both across the colonies.

blocks.title: Locke's idea
blocks.q: In Two Treatises of Government (1689), John Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that government rests on consent. How could colonists use that idea later?
steps: If government exists to protect rights, a government that destroys them loses its claim to obedience.
If government rests on consent, taxes without consent are wrong.
blocks.a: It gave colonists a reason to resist laws they had not consented to; the Declaration of Independence echoes it.

blocks.html: The Awakening also founded colleges to train ministers, among them the College of New Jersey (1746), later Princeton University. Revivals reached enslaved and free Black people too, and many joined Baptist and Methodist churches.

Students sometimes treat the two movements as the same thing. The Awakening was religious revival grounded in personal faith; the Enlightenment stressed reason and science. Be ready to name one figure and one idea for each, and to explain how both, in different ways, taught colonists to question authority.

blocks.html: By 1750 the colonists had more than a century of practice in governing themselves. That experience, from the House of Burgesses to Enlightenment ideas and the loose enforcement of trade laws, explains why later British policies met such resistance.

Colonists governed themselves through elected assemblies (the House of Burgesses from 1619 and an assembly in nearly every colony), town meetings in New England and written plans of government. The assemblies held the power of the purse: they voted the taxes. The Zenger trial (1735) defended printing true criticism of officials.

Self-government grew from distance and neglect as well as principle. London was weeks away by sea, so colonies had to make their own local laws. Most colonies had a governor (chosen by the king or a proprietor), a council and an elected assembly, a pattern that echoed England's king, House of Lords and House of Commons. Because the assembly voted taxes and often the governor's salary, it could bargain with him. Colonists came to see their assemblies as their own small parliaments.

blocks.title: The Dominion of New England
blocks.q: In 1686 King James II merged the New England colonies (later New York and New Jersey too) into one Dominion under Governor Edmund Andros, who ruled without an elected assembly. What happened?
steps: Colonists resented losing their assemblies and charters.
In 1689 news came that James II had been overthrown in England's Glorious Revolution.
Bostonians arrested Andros, and the old colonial governments returned.
blocks.a: The Dominion collapsed in 1689; colonists defended their assemblies and treated the Glorious Revolution as a victory for English liberties.

blocks.title: The Zenger trial
blocks.q: In 1735 the New York printer John Peter Zenger was tried for seditious libel for printing attacks on Governor William Cosby. Under the law then, truth was no defense. What happened?
steps: His lawyer, Andrew Hamilton of Philadelphia, argued that the articles were true and that people may criticize officials truthfully.
The judge told the jury the law was against Zenger.
The jury acquitted him anyway.
blocks.a: Acquittal: an early step toward freedom of the press, though the law itself did not change at once.

blocks.html: A common belief is that colonists had no say in government before 1776. They had elected assemblies for over a century, though only men who owned property could vote. Their protest after 1763 was not for a voice they had never had, but against Parliament taxing them without the consent of those assemblies.

sources.name: OpenStax, U.S. History (Rice University, 2014), Chapter 4, Rule Britannia! The English Empire, 1660–1763

blocks.html: By 1750 the British colonies (Colonial Self-Government) were growing fast and pushing west, toward the Ohio River valley. France claimed that land too, and its forts and Native allies stood in the way. The war that followed decided who would control North America, and its costs led straight to the quarrel that became the Revolution.

Britain and France fought for North America from 1754 to 1763, part of a worldwide war Europeans call the Seven Years' War. Britain won Canada and the land east of the Mississippi. But its huge war debt and the Proclamation of 1763, which closed the land west of the Appalachians to settlers, set the stage for conflict with the colonists.

Winning cost Britain dearly: its national debt nearly doubled, to about 133 million pounds. British leaders reasoned that the colonists, who had gained most from removing the French threat, should help pay for the war and for the soldiers now guarding the frontier. Colonists reasoned that they had fought and paid too, and had always been taxed by their own assemblies. Both sides believed they were being reasonable, which is why the quarrel grew so hard to settle.

events.label: Washington at Fort Necessity; Albany Congress
Treaty of Paris (February); Pontiac's War begins (May)

blocks.title: How the war began
blocks.q: Why did fighting start in the Ohio Country in 1754?
steps: France built forts to link Canada with Louisiana; Virginia also claimed the Ohio valley.
Virginia sent a young officer, George Washington, with troops. In May 1754 his force attacked a French party at Jumonville Glen.
The French struck back and forced Washington to surrender Fort Necessity in July 1754.
blocks.a: Rival claims to the Ohio valley; the clashes of 1754 began a war that spread worldwide.

blocks.title: What the treaty changed
blocks.q: In the Treaty of Paris (February 10, 1763), what did each power gain or lose in North America?
steps: France gave Britain Canada and its land east of the Mississippi (except New Orleans).
France had already given Louisiana west of the Mississippi to its ally Spain.
Spain gave Florida to Britain.
blocks.a: Britain held everything east of the Mississippi; France was gone from the mainland.

blocks.html: The same year, Native nations of the Great Lakes and Ohio valley, led in part by the Ottawa leader Pontiac, rose against British forts (Pontiac's War). Partly to keep peace on the frontier, King George III issued the Proclamation of 1763 (October 7): no colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains. Colonists who had fought to open that land were angry.

blocks.cap: The land between the Appalachians and the Mississippi, which Britain won in 1763, became part of the United States in 1783.

blocks.html: During the war, Benjamin Franklin proposed the Albany Plan of Union (1754), a council of the colonies to raise troops and taxes. The colonial assemblies rejected it; they would not give up their own powers. His cartoon "Join, or Die" was printed with it.

The name misleads. The war was not fought between the French and the Native peoples. The British colonists named it for their enemies: the French and their Indian allies. Many Native nations fought on the French side, others with the British (most of the Haudenosaunee), and many tried to protect their own interests between the two.

blocks.html: After the French and Indian War, Parliament set out to make the colonies pay a share of the empire's costs. Each new law met louder protest, and each protest pushed the two sides to state their principles more sharply.

Parliament passed the Sugar Act (1764), the Stamp Act (1765) and the Townshend Acts (1767). Colonists answered with petitions, the Stamp Act Congress, boycotts and the cry "no taxation without representation."

The quarrel was about who had the right to tax, not how much. British leaders held that Parliament represented every British subject, even those who could not vote for its members ("virtual representation"). Colonists held that they could be taxed only by representatives they had actually elected, and they elected none to Parliament. So any tax laid by Parliament to raise money in the colonies, however small, took their property without their consent.

blocks.title: Why the Stamp Act stirred so much anger
blocks.q: The Sugar Act touched mostly merchants. Why did the Stamp Act anger far more people?
steps: It was a direct tax inside the colonies, not a duty on trade.
It hit lawyers, printers, merchants, tavern keepers and anyone buying a newspaper.
Printers and lawyers were the colonists best able to spread protest.
blocks.a: It touched nearly everyone, especially the people who shaped opinion.

blocks.title: Did protest work?
blocks.q: How did the boycotts of 1765 to 1770 affect British policy?
steps: Colonists refused to buy British goods; women's groups (the Daughters of Liberty) spun homespun cloth in place of British cloth.
British merchants, losing sales, asked Parliament for repeal.
Parliament repealed the Stamp Act (1766) and most Townshend duties (1770), but kept the tax on tea and declared its full authority.
blocks.a: Boycotts won repeal, but Parliament never gave up the principle, so the conflict continued.

blocks.html: Many students think colonists objected mainly to how high the taxes were. Most were small; the Sugar Act actually lowered the molasses tax. The colonists objected that Parliament, in which they had no members, had no right to tax them at all.

blocks.html: The repeal of most Townshend duties in 1770 (New Taxes and Colonial Protest) brought a few calm years, but British troops stayed in Boston and the tea tax remained. Between 1770 and 1774, a chain of events turned protest into open defiance.
Boston Massacre (March 5, 1770) → Tea Act (May 1773) → Boston Tea Party (December 16, 1773) → Coercive (Intolerable) Acts (1774) → First Continental Congress (September 1774).

Each side's response raised the stakes for the other. Colonists destroyed the tea to defend the principle of no taxation without consent. Parliament answered by punishing Boston as a lesson to all, which convinced other colonies that their own rights could be next. A local quarrel in Massachusetts became a cause shared by twelve colonies.

blocks.cap: Put the events in order, then Check.

items: Boston Massacre: on March 5, 1770, British soldiers guarding the customs house fired into a crowd that was taunting them and throwing snowballs and sticks. Five colonists died, among them Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native descent. Paul Revere's engraving showed it as a deliberate slaughter. John Adams defended the soldiers in court; most were acquitted.

Tea Act (1773): to save the struggling East India Company, Parliament let it sell tea directly in the colonies. The tea became cheaper, even with the tax, but buying it meant accepting the tax and a monopoly.
Boston Tea Party: on December 16, 1773, colonists, some disguised as Mohawk Indians, dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor.

Coercive Acts (1774), called the Intolerable Acts by colonists: they closed Boston's port until the tea was paid for, put Massachusetts government under tighter royal control, let royal officials be tried in other colonies or Britain, and widened the quartering of troops.

First Continental Congress: delegates from twelve colonies (all but Georgia) met in Philadelphia from September 5, 1774. They adopted the Continental Association, a boycott of British goods enforced by local committees, and agreed to meet again if their grievances were not addressed.

blocks.title: Why did a cheaper price cause a revolt?
blocks.q: The Tea Act lowered the price of tea. Why did colonists destroy it?
steps: Buying it meant paying the Townshend tea tax and accepting Parliament's right to tax.
The law also gave one company a monopoly, which worried colonial merchants.
blocks.a: The principle of the tax, and the monopoly, not the price.

blocks.html: Two slips are common: putting these events in the wrong order (the Massacre of 1770 came three years before the Tea Party), and thinking the Tea Party protested a tax increase. The Tea Act raised no tax and lowered the price; colonists objected that it kept the tax and favored the East India Company.

blocks.html: By spring 1775, after the Coercive Acts, Massachusetts towns were drilling militia and storing weapons. The British commander in Boston, General Thomas Gage, decided to seize them.

Fighting began at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775. The Second Continental Congress met in May and made George Washington commander of the Continental Army. Thomas Paine's Common Sense (January 1776) argued for full independence.

The war began more than a year before the colonies declared independence. Most colonists in 1775 still saw themselves as British subjects defending their rights. In July 1775, Congress sent the King the Olive Branch Petition, asking for peace. He refused it and in August declared the colonies in rebellion. Paine then gave many colonists a new way to see the crisis: the problem was not bad ministers but monarchy itself, and reconciliation was impossible.

events.label: Congress meets; Bunker Hill; Olive Branch Petition; the King declares a rebellion (May to August)

blocks.title: What happened on April 19, 1775?
blocks.q: Trace the day.
steps: British troops marched from Boston at night to seize militia supplies at Concord.
Riders including Paul Revere and William Dawes spread the alarm.
At dawn at Lexington, shots were fired between the troops and about 70 militiamen; eight militiamen were killed.
At Concord, militia fought the British at the North Bridge; militia fired on the British all the way back to Boston.
blocks.a: The first battles of the war: the British reached Concord but were harried all the way back.

Small islands, not capable of protecting themselves, are the proper objects for government to take under their care; but there is something very absurd, in supposing a Continent to be perpetually governed by an island.

marks.note: Paine calls for independence, not reconciliation.

marks.note: An argument from nature and common sense: a continent should not be ruled by a small, distant island.

blocks.a: A persuasive pamphlet aimed at a wide public at the moment opinion was shifting.

blocks.html: Many people think the war started after the Declaration of Independence. The fighting began in April 1775, more than a year earlier. Through 1775 many colonists hoped only to restore their rights within the empire; the move to independence came in 1776.

blocks.html: By June 1776, after a year of war and after Common Sense, most delegates in Congress were ready to break with Britain. Young learners meet it in The Declaration of Independence; you can read the whole text in the Harvard Classics reading for July 4.

Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776 (the Lee Resolution) and adopted the Declaration on July 4. Written mainly by Thomas Jefferson, it states a theory of government by consent, lists grievances against the King, and declares the colonies free and independent states.

A people breaking away from its government needed to explain itself to the world and to win foreign help, and the Declaration says so: "a decent respect to the opinions of mankind requires that they should declare the causes." Its argument runs like a proof. Premise: people have natural rights, and governments exist to secure them by the consent of the governed. Second premise: the King has repeatedly violated those rights (the grievances). Conclusion: the people may "alter or abolish" that government, so the colonies are free.

blocks.title: Who wrote it?
blocks.q: Who drafted the Declaration, and was it changed?
steps: Congress named a Committee of Five: Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman and Robert Livingston.
Jefferson wrote the draft; Adams and Franklin suggested edits.
Congress cut and changed parts of the draft, including a long passage blaming the King for the slave trade.
blocks.a: Jefferson wrote it; the committee and Congress revised it. Most delegates signed the engrossed copy on August 2, 1776; 56 men signed in all.

blocks.html: The Declaration did not set up the new government. It explains why the colonies separated. The government was set up first by the Articles of Confederation (in force 1781) and then by the Constitution (1789). A quick check: the Declaration has no rules for Congress, courts or elections.

blocks.html: The Declaration spoke for "one people," but the colonists were deeply divided. The Revolution was also a civil war, fought between neighbors and within families.

Patriots backed independence; Loyalists stayed loyal to Britain; many people tried to stay neutral. Historians estimate that roughly 15 to 20 percent of white colonists were Loyalists. Dunmore's Proclamation (1775) offered freedom to enslaved people of rebel owners who joined the British, and most Native nations sided with Britain.

People chose sides for many reasons: principle, but also where they lived, what they owned, whom they trusted and who seemed likely to protect them. Royal officials, Anglican clergy and some merchants with ties to Britain often stayed loyal. Some backcountry farmers resented the coastal elites who led the Patriots. For enslaved people and Native nations, the question was which side offered the better chance of freedom or of keeping their land.

marks.note: Only people owned by Patriots: Loyalists' enslaved workers were not offered freedom.

marks.note: The aim was military: to weaken the rebellion and add soldiers.

blocks.title: Who answered Dunmore?
blocks.q: What happened after Dunmore's Proclamation of November 7, 1775?
steps: Hundreds of enslaved people escaped to the British lines in Virginia; some formed the "Ethiopian Regiment."
Many died of smallpox in the camps.
In 1779 the British commander Henry Clinton made a wider offer (the Philipsburg Proclamation).
Patriot slaveholders were alarmed, and some colonists who had been unsure turned against Britain.
blocks.a: Thousands of enslaved people sought freedom with the British during the war; the offer also hardened Patriot feeling.

blocks.title: Native nations choose
blocks.q: Why did most Native nations side with Britain?
steps: Britain's Proclamation of 1763 had tried to keep settlers east of the mountains.
Patriot settlers were the ones pressing onto Native land.
The Haudenosaunee split: the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant led warriors for Britain, while the Oneida and Tuscarora mostly aided the Patriots.
blocks.a: Britain looked like the better protector of their lands; but nations, and even the Haudenosaunee, divided.

blocks.html: About 5,000 Black men served on the Patriot side, many from New England. After the war, some 60,000 to 80,000 Loyalists left the United States, many for Canada; the British also evacuated thousands of Black Loyalists, some to Nova Scotia.

The common picture is of a whole people rising together. In fact only part of the population actively backed independence; perhaps a fifth or less were Loyalists, and many others tried to stay out of the war. The numbers also changed over the war as armies came and went.

blocks.html: Britain had the world's strongest navy, a professional army and far more money. The Continental Army (formed in 1775) was often short of food, pay and training. How did the Americans win?

Key moments: Washington's victory at Trenton (December 26, 1776); the American win at Saratoga (October 1777) that brought the French alliance (February 1778); the hard winter at Valley Forge (1777 to 1778); and the British surrender at Yorktown (October 19, 1781).

The Americans did not need to conquer Britain; they needed to survive until Britain gave up. Britain had to defeat a rebellion spread across a thousand miles of coast, supplied across an ocean. Washington's strategy was to keep his army in existence, avoid a fatal defeat, and strike when he could. Each year the war went on, it cost Britain more. Saratoga showed the world that Americans could beat a British army, and France, Britain's old rival, joined the war, later with Spain as France's ally. French money, soldiers and above all ships turned the balance.

blocks.cap: Some places of the war. After 1778 the main fighting moved south.

blocks.title: Why was Saratoga the turning point?
blocks.q: In October 1777 the British general John Burgoyne surrendered his army at Saratoga, New York. Why did it matter so much?
steps: Burgoyne had marched south from Canada to cut New England off; the plan failed.
More than 6,000 British and German soldiers surrendered on October 17, 1777.
The victory convinced France that the Americans could win; France signed the Treaty of Alliance on February 6, 1778.
blocks.a: It brought France into the war.

blocks.title: Why did Cornwallis surrender at Yorktown?
blocks.q: In 1781 General Cornwallis's army was at Yorktown, Virginia, on the coast. What trapped it?
steps: A French fleet under Admiral de Grasse won control of Chesapeake Bay (September 5, 1781), so the British navy could not rescue or supply Cornwallis.
About 16,000 American and French troops under Washington and Rochambeau besieged the town.
Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781.
blocks.a: Land siege plus French sea power: neither alone would have been enough.

blocks.html: At Valley Forge (December 1777 to June 1778), some 1,700 to 2,500 soldiers died, mostly of disease. There, the Prussian officer Baron von Steuben drilled the army into a more disciplined force.

The Americans did not win mainly by beating the British in great battles; they lost many, including New York (1776) and Charleston (1780). They won by keeping the army alive, winning key fights at the right time, and gaining French money, troops and ships. After Yorktown, Britain decided the war was not worth its cost.

blocks.html: After Yorktown in October 1781, fighting dwindled, but the war was not over. British troops still held New York, Charleston and Savannah, and peace had to be negotiated in Europe. You can read the treaty in the Harvard Classics reading for September 3.

In the Treaty of Paris, signed September 3, 1783, Britain recognized American independence. The borders: the Mississippi River in the west, roughly the Great Lakes and Canada in the north, and Florida (returned to Spain) in the south, at the 31st parallel.

blocks.html: The American negotiators, Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay, won generous terms. Britain's new government under Lord Shelburne wanted a quick peace and hoped to pull the United States away from France and toward British trade. A large, friendly United States seemed better for Britain than a small one tied to France. So Britain gave up the land all the way to the Mississippi.

blocks.title: What else did the treaty say?
blocks.q: Besides independence and borders, what did the treaty promise?
steps: American fishermen could keep fishing off Newfoundland.
Debts owed to British merchants were to be paid.
Congress would "earnestly recommend" that the states return Loyalists' seized property.
Both nations could navigate the Mississippi.
blocks.a: Fishing rights, debts, a recommendation on Loyalist property and use of the Mississippi.

blocks.title: Who was left out?
blocks.q: Native nations held most of the land between the Appalachians and the Mississippi. What did the treaty say about them?
steps: Nothing: they were not part of the negotiations.
Britain transferred its claims to land that Native nations still lived on and controlled.
Conflict over that land continued for decades.
blocks.a: They were left out, and the treaty set up new struggles over their lands.

blocks.html: Congress ratified the treaty on January 14, 1784. The last British troops left New York in November 1783.

A frequent error is to think the war ended with Yorktown in 1781. Fighting dwindled after Yorktown, but the war formally ended with the Treaty of Paris two years later, in 1783. Remember both dates: Yorktown 1781, peace 1783.

blocks.html: The Treaty of Paris made the United States independent. But was the Revolution only a change of rulers, or did it change American society? This is a classic question of change and continuity, and historians still debate how radical the Revolution was.

The Revolution brought new state constitutions with bills of rights, the gradual abolition of slavery in Northern states (beginning with Pennsylvania in 1780), Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom (1786) and new ideas about women as "republican mothers." Change was real but uneven.

Revolutionaries had justified independence with claims about natural rights, equality and consent. Once stated, those ideas could be turned on American practices. Enslaved people petitioned for freedom using the language of the Declaration; dissenting churches demanded an end to state-supported religion; some women asked for a voice. Where interests allowed, the new states changed. Where powerful interests resisted, as with slavery in the South, they did not.

blocks.title: Read a law closely
blocks.q: Pennsylvania's act of March 1, 1780, was the first law in the United States to begin ending slavery. Did it free everyone at once?
steps: It banned bringing new enslaved people into the state.
Children born to enslaved mothers after the law were not to be enslaved for life, but would serve until age 28.
People already enslaved stayed enslaved.
blocks.a: No. It was gradual: slavery in Pennsylvania ended over decades.

blocks.title: Freedom through the courts
blocks.q: How did slavery end in Massachusetts?
steps: The 1780 Massachusetts constitution declared all men "born free and equal."
In 1781 Elizabeth Freeman (Mum Bett) sued for her freedom and won before a jury.
In later cases the courts held that slavery could not stand under that constitution, and by the 1790 census no enslaved people were recorded in the state.
blocks.a: Through lawsuits brought by enslaved people under the new state constitution.

blocks.html: In March 1776, Abigail Adams wrote to her husband John asking Congress to "Remember the Ladies" in the new laws. The historian Linda Kerber (1976) named the new ideal of the educated, patriotic mother who raises virtuous citizens "republican motherhood."

Avoid both extremes: that the Revolution changed everything, or that it changed nothing for those left out. Northern states began ending slavery while Southern states kept it, and voting stayed mostly limited to men with property. Historians disagree about the balance: some stress how radical the new ideas of equality were; others stress how much stayed the same.

blocks.html: In what the Revolution changed you saw the new states write constitutions of their own. They also needed a government for all thirteen together. Congress drafted the Articles of Confederation in 1777, and they took effect on March 1, 1781, once Maryland, the last state, ratified them. They were the country's first constitution.

The Articles made a league of states, not a strong nation. There was one body, Congress, where each state had one vote. There was no president and no national courts. Congress could not tax: it could only ask the states for money. Key laws needed nine of the thirteen states, and changing the Articles needed all thirteen.

The weakness was on purpose. Americans had just fought a war against a distant government that taxed them without their consent. They feared any central power that could do the same, so they kept power in the states, closer to the people. The Articles say so plainly: each state "retains its sovereignty, freedom, and independence."

blocks.title: Reading a weakness from the rules
blocks.q: In 1781 and again in 1783, Congress asked the states to let it collect a 5 percent tax on imports. Twelve states agreed to the first plan; Rhode Island alone said no. Why did one state's "no" kill it?
steps: A tax power would change the Articles, so it was an amendment.
Amendments needed the approval of every state legislature: all thirteen.
Rhode Island refused in 1782, so the plan died; the second plan failed the same way.
Without a tax, Congress depended on what the states chose to send, and most sent far less than they were asked.
blocks.a: Changing the Articles needed all thirteen states, so a single state could block it.

blocks.html: It is easy to think the Articles did nothing. Under them Congress won the war, made the Treaty of Paris (1783), and organized the western lands with the Land and Northwest Ordinances. The trouble was narrower: a Congress that could not tax or enforce its laws. Quick check: if a claim says "the Articles failed at everything," ask how the war was won and the West organized.

By the mid-1780s those limits hurt. Congress could not pay its war debts or its soldiers. States taxed one another's goods. Britain kept forts on American soil, and Spain closed the lower Mississippi River to American trade. Leaders began to ask for a stronger union.

blocks.html: The Articles of Confederation gave Congress a big job: the land between the Appalachian Mountains and the Mississippi River that Britain gave up in 1783. Several states claimed parts of it. By the mid-1780s they had handed most of those claims to Congress. Two laws settled how the land would be sold and governed.

The Land Ordinance of 1785 surveyed the land into square townships, six miles on a side, each cut into 36 sections of one square mile (640 acres), and set one section in each township aside for schools. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 set the steps from territory to state: new states would join "on an equal footing with the original States," and slavery was banned in the Northwest Territory.

A grid made land easy to sell: a buyer could name an exact square, and the sales gave the nearly broke Congress money. The path to statehood mattered even more. The old states could have ruled the West as their own colonies, the way Britain had ruled them. Instead the Ordinance promised that new states would be full partners. Every state since has joined on those terms.

blocks.title: Reading Article 6
blocks.q: Article 6 of the Northwest Ordinance says: "There shall be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude in the said territory, otherwise than in the punishment of crimes." What did it do, and what did it leave out?
steps: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude": no one could be held as a slave in the territory.
"Otherwise than in the punishment of crimes": forced labor as a punishment for a crime was still allowed.
The same article required that people escaping slavery from the original states be returned.
It covered only the land north and west of the Ohio River. Land south of the river was left open to slavery.
blocks.a: It banned slavery north of the Ohio River, with exceptions for criminal punishment and a duty to return people who escaped.

blocks.html: Some students think new western states joined as lesser members, like colonies of the original thirteen. The Ordinance says the opposite: new states are admitted "on an equal footing with the original States in all respects whatever." Quick check: does Ohio have fewer senators than Virginia? No. Both have two.

The Ordinance also promised that "the utmost good faith shall always be observed towards the Indians" and that their land would not be taken without their consent except in "just and lawful wars." In practice, the nations of the Ohio country, among them the Shawnee, Miami and Delaware, fought a long war against settlement, and most of their land was taken by treaties made after defeats.

blocks.html: The Articles left the hard money problems to the states. After the war, Massachusetts owed large debts, and it raised taxes and demanded they be paid in hard money (gold and silver coin), which few farmers had. Courts took farms and jailed debtors who could not pay. Many of those farmers were veterans who had fought the Revolution.

In 1786 and 1787, armed farmers in western Massachusetts, many of them veterans and one of them a former captain named Daniel Shays, closed county courts so that no more farms could be taken. In January 1787 they marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield and were driven off by militia. Congress had no army to send and no money to raise one, and that worried leaders in every state.

Why did a local revolt matter so much? It showed two things at once. First, ordinary people were in real distress after the war. Second, the national government could not keep order even at its own arsenal: the Massachusetts militia was paid for by loans from Boston merchants. To many leaders, including George Washington, it was proof that the Articles were too weak. Months later, delegates met in Philadelphia.
